“We lost by two points,” Baljeet said, dropping his bag. “It's my fault. I missed the last shot.”

“Baljeet,” said Sangeeta, the captain, “I called the last play. I chose to give you the ball because the defenders were on Ritu. That's on me too.”

“But I missed.”

“And Ritu ran eight minutes of defence, Farah scored twelve, and you made five assists. That's how we got to the last shot at all.”

Farah smiled. Ritu looked up. “I was tired in the last quarter. I should have said I needed a rest.”

“Then we all learn,” said Sangeeta. “Next practice: last-play drills, and anyone can call for a sub.”

Baljeet let out a breath. “Okay.”

“Ma'am, ma'am, I know this one—” Noor blurted, half out of the seat, on Nandini's second day as a Class 8 teacher.
“Noor, I'm glad you know. Hand up, please, and I'll come to you next.” Noor sat down, red-faced, hand raised.
“Ma'am, yesterday you let Rohan shout out,” said a boy at the back.

Madhav, sit. You keep saying “it's fine” about your project partner, and I remember saying the same. I'm Payal. When I was twenty-five, my colleague Gaurav borrowed my files without asking, interrupted me in meetings and left dirty cups on my desk. I smiled at all of it for two months. row_description: A child is told by an older student or adult to hide something, pick on someone or keep a secret. They feel a pull between obedience and a stomach-sinking sense of wrongness.

row_description: A dependable colleague is given extra work because they will always deliver, while others coast. They feel used, but often also proud of being needed, a mixed state.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative in a rural or small-town Indian setting (village, farm, kasba, local bus, temple fair, small shop).

record.passage: In a small-town post office, Ishita balanced the day's accounts by four, as usual. The postmaster handed her the pension registers as well. "You never make mistakes, Ishita." row_description: A college student holds back questions in a big hall for fear of seeming ignorant. They often find that others had the same question and are grateful when someone asks it.

record.passage: The projector had died fifteen minutes into the lecture, so the professor was explaining eigenvalues on the whiteboard for three hundred students, and the back rows could barely hear. Jyoti had a question about the second example and kept it inside for forty minutes. Beside her, Sarita was doodling. “Last question,” the professor said, checking the clock. Jyoti's heart thudded. Behind her someone breathed out, “Thank God, I had the same one.” Two more students called out follow-ups. Sarita looked up from the doodle, grinning, and tapped Jyoti's notebook.

qa.a: There were three hundred students.

qa.a: Jyoti seems afraid of seeming ignorant in front of a huge hall, since her heart thudded and her voice cracked when she finally asked.

qa.a: She could write the question down early, sit near the front or ask a neighbour first, and use the last-question slot rather than waiting until the end.

qa.q: What might the person behind Jyoti have felt when saying, “Thank God, I had the same one”?
qa.a: That person probably felt relieved and grateful that Jyoti asked it, since they had held the same doubt without saying it.

record.grounding: A college student holds back a question in a large hall for fear of seeming ignorant and finds that others had the same question.

row_description: A child stops admitting they like a certain cartoon or song once classmates mock it. They feel a small betrayal of themselves but relief at not standing out.

qa.a: Meera may feel uneasy; looking at her tiffin and saying nothing suggests she does not want to join in but also does not want to be the next target.

row_description: A toddler stops or goes on according to the caregiver's face and tone. They obey the emotional signal more than the words, which is how authority is first felt.
recipe_text: An observer's account: a neighbour, sibling, classmate or colleague describes what they saw, without knowing the protagonist's inner state for sure.

record.passage: From my balcony I watch the courtyard most evenings. Hansa, about two, was touching the gate latch while her father Nilesh chatted with two other parents. Nilesh lifted her and rubbed her back.

qa.a: Nilesh said "No, Hansa" laughing, and later said the same words in a flat, firm voice.

row_description: A teenager is told that skipping class, vaping or a prank is what everyone does, with a hint of exclusion if they refuse. The threat is social, so it feels bigger than the act itself.
recipe_text: First-person reflective account by the protagonist, looking back a little (for 7-12 keep it simple and short).

record.passage: My name is Farida, and I remember the exact tone of Rafiq's voice at the gate. "Everyone is skipping the last two periods. You coming or what?" Five of them stood in a half-circle, Rafiq in the middle, the rest nodding. Nasreen looked at her shoes. Nobody said what would happen if I refused, but Rafiq added, "We'll just tell you about it after." That was the threat. My chest tightened as if I would lose the whole group, not just an afternoon. I said, "Not today, I have to submit my file." It was true, and a little less than the whole truth. They left. I sat in class with my heart thudding, and an hour later Nasreen sent one 👍.

qa.a: Rafiq said, "We'll just tell you about it after."

qa.a: Farida gave a plain reason and stayed in class; next time Farida could also tell a trusted adult or Nasreen how pressured it felt.

record.grounding: A teenager is told that skipping class is what everyone does, with a hint of exclusion, and the social threat feels bigger than the act.

row_description: An employee who finds a safety or ethics problem is advised by superiors to let it go for the company's sake. They feel fear for their job and doubt about their own judgement.

record.passage:
The rice mill outside town was loud by seven. Near the drying floor Kishore noticed bare wires hanging above wet sacks. He told the supervisor.
“Let it go,” the supervisor said, glancing at the door. “The owner’s inspection is tomorrow, and the mill can’t afford a shutdown before harvest. It’s been like that for months.”

That evening Kishore wrote the date and the place in his pocket notebook, and stared at the page for a long time.

qa.a: Tejas may have been worried about the danger and about losing wages. Muttering and saying no more suggests he was torn.

record.grounding: Shows an employee who finds a safety problem being told to let it go for the mill, feeling fear for the job and doubt.

row_description: An employee is asked to backdate a form or smooth a report and complies, telling themselves it is not their decision. Diffused responsibility lets ordinary people do things they would never choose alone.

record.subtype: Following a boss into a grey area [Actor]

qa.a: Naveen told Samir personal responsibility remains and to ask for such requests in writing, and raised the report with the head of quality the same day so the readings could be restored.
